name: Elevated head sleeping / wedge pillow

lead: A wedge pillow or bed risers keep the head above the body while you sleep. Users raise their head to wake with a less puffy face, especially around the eyes.

The chain is simple: with the head raised, less fluid pools in the face while lying flat, so there is less morning puffiness. Head-of-bed elevation is an established lifestyle measure for reflux, and reference sources suggest it may limit fluid shifting around the eyes. No trial has tested it for facial appearance.

paras: Users place a foam wedge under the upper body or put risers under the head end of the bed and sleep that way nightly. It takes a few nights to adjust to, and it is often combined with low evening salt and alcohol.
Low risk. Some people get neck or back discomfort or slide down the wedge, and a wedge that raises only the head can bend the neck.

angle.text: Sleeping with the head raised on a wedge or risers keeps fluid from pooling in the face overnight, so users wake with less puffiness. Head-of-bed elevation is an established measure for reflux, and its effect on facial puffiness has not been tested.

lead: Sleeping with the head raised, using a wedge pillow or bed risers, is said by looksmaxxing communities to reduce morning facial puffiness from fluid pooling. Head-of-bed elevation is an established lifestyle measure for reflux.[1][2]
Reference sources suggest elevation may limit fluid shifting around the eyes, but no trials were found testing wedge pillows for facial appearance.[3]

paras: A 2021 systematic review evaluated head-of-bed elevation for reflux symptoms in adults.[1] A 2026 noninferiority randomised trial compared adding a wedge pillow with an evening proton pump inhibitor for nocturnal reflux.[2]
A 2014 study of 30 people found a 20-degree head-up position affected nocturnal intraocular pressure compared with lying flat.[4]
Encyclopaedic sources note that eye swelling is most obvious after waking, possibly from fluid shifting while lying flat, and that elevating the head may prevent this.[3]
No studies found for facial puffiness. Trials exist for reflux, as above.[1][2]
